Adult Shortspine thornyhead (Sebastolobus alascanus) are among the larger scorpionfishes inhabiting the continental slope of the North Pacific, with the largest individuals attaining an ultimate total length of 80 centimeters [Li = 80 centimeters]. This species is characterized by a slow-growth, long-lived life history strategy typical of many deepwater teleosts. Field surveys indicate that sexual maturation begins only after individuals reach a total length of approximately 22 centimeters [Lp = approximately 22 centimeters], a size that corresponds to several years of growth in the cold, food-limited deep-sea environment. The mass of a female at the onset of puberty has been estimated at 123.6 grams [Wwp = 123.6 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships established for specimens collected during NOAA trawl surveys. In stark contrast, the mass of a fully developed, senescent adult can exceed 7.3 kilograms, with the maximum recorded adult wet weight reaching approximately 7300 grams [Wwi = approximately 7300 grams]. This nearly sixty-fold increase in somatic mass from maturation to senescence underscores the prolonged period of indeterminate growth that defines this and other deepwater rockfish species.

Reproductive output in Shortspine thornyhead is tightly coupled to the cold, stable thermal regime of their demersal habitat, which typically hovers near 3.8 °C [T = 3.8 °C]. At this temperature, a female's maximum annual reproductive output is considerable, beginning with the production of multiple egg batches each season. Individual females release an average of 2250 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 2250 eggs per spawning event], and they may spawn as many as two times per year [F_R_i = two times per year] under favorable foraging conditions. This strategy yields a high potential fecundity, though actual recruitment is likely limited by the low survival rates typical of pelagic larvae in oligotrophic waters. The temperature dependence of gametogenesis and ovulation is pronounced; below 3.8 °C [T = 3.8 °C], vitellogenesis slows markedly, and spawning intervals lengthen. Available data suggest that even a modest warming of bottom waters could accelerate ovarian development, potentially altering the timing and magnitude of annual egg production in this stenothermal species.

The initial mass of a newly fertilized egg is remarkably small, reflecting the tiny size at which this species begins its life. Each fertilized ovum, which measures approximately 0.8 millimeters in diameter, has a calculated wet weight of just 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], a value consistent with the minimal yolk reserves typical of pelagic spawners. These minute, transparent eggs are released into the water column where they drift as part of the ichthyoplankton for several weeks. Embryonic development proceeds slowly at the ambient temperatures of the deep sea, and the yolk-sac larva that emerges at eclosion is itself a minute, endotrophic organism dependent on endogenous nutrients until the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding begins. The energetic constraints imposed by such a small starting mass are substantial; larvae must locate and capture suitably sized planktonic prey within days of yolk-sack resorption or face starvation. This early bottleneck represents a critical period in the species' life history, filtering out the vast majority of offspring before settlement.

The maximum lifespan of Shortspine thornyhead is exceptionally long, with the oldest documented individuals reaching 100 years [am = 100 years] under the consistently cold conditions of their habitat, typically at a temperature of 3.8 °C [T = 3.8 °C]. This remarkable longevity is one of the most extended recorded among Pacific scorpionfishes and is comparable to that of the closely related longspine thornyhead (Sebastolobus altivelis). Such extreme lifespan is thought to be an evolutionary response to the low and erratic recruitment success typical of deep-sea environments, where years may pass between favorable settlement events. The very low metabolic demand at cold temperatures reduces cellular damage rates and slows senescence, allowing individuals to accumulate biomass and reproductive potential over many decades. Tagging and otolith microstructure studies have confirmed that growth continues throughout life, although the annual increment becomes vanishingly small in the oldest age classes. This life-history pattern, characterized by late maturity, low fecundity relative to body size, and extreme longevity, renders the species particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as the removal of large, old individuals can take many decades to replace.

Comparative physiological studies have examined how metabolic performance in Sebastolobus alascanus scales with body size across the full range from first-feeding larvae to senescent adults. The 0.000268 gram [Wwb = 0.000268 gram] mass of the yolk-sac larva places it among the smallest teleost hatchlings, demanding a high mass-specific metabolic rate to support rapid growth of the feeding apparatus. As growth proceeds, the mass-specific oxygen consumption declines while absolute metabolic demand rises, reaching a peak in the large, 7300 gram [Wwi = 7300 gram] adults that cruise the benthic boundary layer. Interestingly, the 123.6 gram [Wwp = 123.6 gram] mass at puberty represents a functionally significant body size at which the trade-off between somatic investment and reproductive allocation shifts, as the energetic cost of egg production becomes a non-trivial fraction of the daily energy budget. At the habitat temperature of 3.8 °C [T = 3.8 °C], routine metabolic rates are approximately half those measured in confamilial species from shallower, warmer waters.
